decisions.reason: SOL keeps the approaching danger and its uncontrollable nature while preserving the narration’s voice.
“Draw closer” keeps the image of Dark Heaven approaching.
The standalone sentence preserves the reveal that another blaze is coming from behind.
“Its heat” clearly refers to the second blaze and keeps the internal-burning image.
The source says the pill was newly improved; SOL drops “newly.”
The source says it is no longer a simple blaze; SOL drops “simple.”
The source specifies that the time bomb suddenly explodes; SOL omits “suddenly.”
SOL preserves the drug-addiction comparison and the inability to stop in natural English.
Dropping “a bunch of” does not change the claim that martial artists are lunatics willing to do anything to grow stronger.
“Desire to master martial arts” preserves the source’s desire for martial arts and its danger.
“Grim murmur” conveys the weight of Jeok Cheongang’s remark without changing its effect.
“He was right” makes clear Jeok Cheongang’s diagnosis is being affirmed.
SOL preserves desire as poison that even the Myriad-Poison Ring cannot cure.
“Bumpkin mountain bandit” retains the dismissive description of the one person who has not understood.
“Looked thoroughly confused” preserves Jang Il’s evident confusion.
The unanswered question remains clear from the surrounding exchange; SOL does not alter the event.
The guides stiffen and reply, preserving the key reaction and action.
“Glad to hear it” keeps the speaker’s pleased response to being offered obedience.
The Korean gives the narrator as the speaker; SOL changes the subject to “we.”
“Get the word out” naturally preserves the urgency of spreading the information.
SOL retains the lost-half-his-mind detail and the possibility that interrogation could yield important information.
“Nangong Cheon had sent four guides with us” preserves the source’s assignment and number.
“What we’ve learned” fits the instruction to report this fact without overstating it as everything.
The quick understanding and ease of passing along the message remain intact.
“Every soldier he can” and the investigation instructions preserve the City Lord’s assigned duties.
A thorough investigation turning up traces preserves the source’s point that digging would reveal evidence.
SOL preserves the City Lord’s troop count and ability to search areas beyond the Nangong Family’s reach.
“Go that far for us” naturally conveys the concern that the City Lord may not cooperate.
The source is hedged—“I thought I knew”—while SOL states certainty.
The reordered clause preserves the long-standing noninterference between government and Murim.
SOL preserves the Emperor’s backing of the Murim Alliance as a cooperative arrangement.
The source says the City Lord would dislike hearing this; SOL narrows it to hearing an order.
SOL preserves the mutual indifference between officials and martial artists and the effectively order-like request.
The elliptical “He might not” naturally completes the preceding doubt about the City Lord’s cooperation.
The source explicitly identifies the speaker as a Nangong Family martial artist; SOL drops that binding group name.
“This’ll do” fits the decision to use cloth instead of paper.
SOL adds that it is the narrator’s horse, which the source does not specify.
“Gave a silent command” preserves the narrator’s unspoken instruction.
The source describes a cool sensation reaching the hand; SOL changes this to an object appearing in it.
The contraction preserves the same brief, surprised question.
The questioning look preserves the martial artist’s puzzled reaction as the narrator heats the object.
“Hummm” better conveys the source’s resonant buzzing sound than “Rumble.”
SOL preserves the plaque heating red-hot and the engraved characters heating with it.
The source says the plaque meets the silk; SOL adds the more forceful action of pressing it.
SOL retains the acrid smoke and the mark left on the cloth without changing the result.
“They’ll be able to make it out” naturally conveys that the imprint is legible.
The source’s “before I knew it” marks the suddenness of everyone staring; SOL drops that timing beat.
SOL preserves the instruction to show the City Lord the token and make clear it is an order, not a request.
The gaping reaction is already established; this concise line preserves their continued shock.
“Acts offended” preserves the condition of showing displeasure, and “word for word” keeps the exact-message instruction.
SOL preserves the trembling question and the narrator’s immediate answer.
“Nest-building dragons” naturally preserves the fantasy-world image.
The blunt command preserves the universal rule and its force.
The revised question preserves the narrator’s curiosity about the City Lord’s official rank.
SOL combines the thought and its conclusion while preserving the rank comparison.
The rank-comparison sentence is retained in H055, so this duplicate hunk is correctly removed.
“후발대” means reinforcements or a follow-up force, not merely a group following them.
“Clamped shut” naturally preserves the mouths closing after moments of shock.
The source identifies the speaker as one of the Nangong Family martial artists; SOL omits that binding group name.
The speaker asks about reinforcements; “the group following you” changes what he is asking about.
“People from” preserves that the reinforcements come from the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
The source says to act if the City Lord seems very suspicious; SOL drops that intensity.
The source says the City Lord could not be harboring other intentions; “treacherous” makes those intentions specifically disloyal.
The source asks whether this is allowed; SOL changes the question to whether the narrator can do it.
The dazed question and calm answer remain clear without repeating the speaker’s identity.
The source first confirms “It is” and then adds “I can”; SOL drops the confirmation.
“We were at war” preserves the wartime context and the sentence remains faithful to the narrator’s authority.
The source says both authority and prestige derive from the Emperor; SOL omits prestige.
The source says “this sword”; SOL changes the deictic reference to “that sword.”
SOL preserves the purpose of the sword and title: defeating enemies in the way and protecting the narrator’s people.
The willingness to keep fighting with a sword until collapse preserves the source’s exhaustion image.
The jolting saddles preserve the movement under the riders as they stare blankly.
“Wheeled their horses around” preserves the turn and departure toward their destinations.
The remaining guide and the temporarily forgotten person are both preserved.
The delayed reply still comes from behind the narrator.
SOL preserves Jang Il’s unnecessary determination without changing the reaction.
“Get off” naturally conveys the order to dismount in this scene.
“Lived through war” preserves the experience required to recognize wartime signs.
The source specifically locates the air around them; SOL drops that spatial detail.
“Was different from usual” preserves the source’s observation.
The source states that ominous dark energy ripples around them; SOL weakens this with “something” and “seemed.”
“Couldn’t relax” naturally preserves the old man’s troubled state after his long sleep.
SOL preserves the imagined observer’s scoff and judgment that the old man is senile without adding profanity.
“Strong sunlight” preserves the intense sunlight pouring through the scattered clouds.
The conditional preserves both kinds of people who would not dare meet his eyes.
The recast preserves the old man’s size, reputation, and status as a living legend.
“Even a beast’s quietest roar” preserves the point that even a small roar can shake its surroundings.
The old man’s anger that nobody woke him is preserved in direct, natural dialogue.
The Korean leaves the person outside’s gender unspecified; SOL assigns him a masculine pronoun.
“Got an excuse?” preserves the blunt challenge in natural speech.
The source’s specific threat to rearrange the five viscera and six bowels is reduced to generic “organs” in SOL.
SOL retains his poor sleep, irritability, and forgotten threat in natural prose.
The source says he finally slept well and infers something must have happened; SOL changes this to a present-tense general complaint.
The reordered sentence preserves the quiet tongue-click and the old man getting up.
The source says he knows what kind of men they are; SOL omits that characterization.
The men’s lack of sense and the seriousness implied by their meeting remain intact.
The Inner Hall destination and instruction to announce his arrival are explicit in the source.
“Grew deep and grave” preserves the old man’s gaze settling into a profound, serious expression.
